title: Finite Gysin costalk comparisons commute with higher residues
statement:
Let $\ell$ be prime, $n\geq1$, $\Lambda=\mathbf Z/\ell^n\mathbf Z$, and $f:T\to S$ a finite morphism of Noetherian excellent schemes on which $\ell$ is invertible [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism, def-exc-excellent-ring]. Work in small etale $D^+$ with costalks $C_{\bar s}$, roots-of-unity twists and geometric specializations as in [def-per-potential-dualizing-complex], and higher transitions as in [lem-per-higher-residue-transitivity]. Let $f^!$ be the right adjoint of $f_*=Rf_!$ [def-amb-etale-compact-support]. For $t\mapsto s$, let $a_t:\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(t)\to\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(s)$ be the residue-field map. Let $$B_{f,t,M}:a_t^*C_sM\xrightarrow{\sim}C_t(f^!M)$$ be the isomorphism of [lem-per-finite-residue-gysin-naturality]: the finite-field Gysin map $\operatorname{Cl}_{a_t}\otimes1$, the field tensor map onto $a_t^!C_sM$, and the inverse supported-transitivity identification $a_t^!C_sM\simeq C_t(f^!M)$. For immediate specializations on both schemes the square below is the square of that lemma; the present assertion extends it to arbitrary codimension.
The finite-field Gysin comparison is normalized as in the induced pinnings of [lem-per-putative-finite-detection]: it is the canonical etale identification for a finite separable extension and multiplication by its degree for a finite purely inseparable extension. For every $M\in D^+(S_{\mathrm{et}},\Lambda)$, every $j\in\mathbf Z$, and every geometric specialization $\bar t'\rightsquigarrow\bar t$ above $\bar s'\rightsquigarrow\bar s$ of codimension $c$ on both schemes, one has
$$\operatorname{sp}^{T,j}_{\bar t',\bar t}\circ H^j(B_{f,t',M})=H^{j+2c}(B_{f,t,M}(c))\circ\operatorname{sp}^{S,j}_{\bar s',\bar s}.$$
The lower costalks are read at the geometric points induced by the given lifts. These comparisons commute with cochain shifts, signed Tate twists, and etale restriction, localization and strict localization. In particular, for a closed immersion, $B$ is the supported-composition identification, and it identifies the higher residue maps on the closed subscheme with those on the ambient scheme for specializations in that closed subscheme.

source.place: Expose XVII, Theorem 3.1.2, Proposition 3.3.1 and Proposition 3.5.4 (the commuting finite-Gysin square); localization as in section 3.5 and Lemma 3.5.5.

proof.text: Use exactly the map $B$ of [lem-per-finite-residue-gysin-naturality], which is an isomorphism for arbitrary $M\in D^+$ with our prime-power coefficients. Its field tensor map is the particular counit-defined map of [lem-per-field-exceptional-tensor], not an unspecified isomorphism. The class normalization can also be checked directly: for a finite separable field extension the map is smooth of relative dimension zero, so [lem-per-noetherian-prime-power-smooth-duality] identifies its orientation and tensor comparison with the etale adjunction comparison. For a purely inseparable extension, [lem-per-prime-power-regular-gysin] identifies the class with multiplication by the field degree. That degree is a power of the residue characteristic, hence a unit modulo $\ell^n$. For a general finite extension combine these two cases by the composition identity for the Gysin class and for the tensor map in the latter node and [lem-per-field-exceptional-tensor]. Thus no unscaled identification is substituted for the specified Gysin comparison.

source.place: XVII, Proposition 2.4.3.1 and Remark 2.4.3.2; Proposition 3.3.1, vertical arrows; XVI Gysin composition

proof.text: We first check that a factorization upstairs projects to one of the same successive codimensions downstairs. By [lem-trf-finite-base-strict-localization], the map $T_{(\bar v)}\to S_{(f\bar v)}$ is finite and local. Write it as $\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}A$. If the image of the general geometric point has prime $\mathfrak q$ in $B$, put $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\cap A$. The reduced closures in these strict localizations are $\operatorname{Spec}(B/\mathfrak q)$ and $\operatorname{Spec}(A/\mathfrak p)$. The map $A/\mathfrak p\hookrightarrow B/\mathfrak q$ is injective and finite: images of finitely many $A$-module generators of $B$ still generate its quotient. It is therefore integral by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-algebra-is-integral]; the finite-module description is [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism]. By [lem-weil-pbc-integral-injective-dimension-equal] these closures have equal dimensions. These dimensions are precisely the two geometric codimensions. Apply this calculation to each arrow of a chosen geometric chain. In particular codimension-one arrows stay immediate and codimension-zero arrows stay transports. The projected geometric arrows have the specified composite because all the maps of strict localizations commute with $f$. This calculation requires no global dimension function and no surjectivity of $f$.

source.place: XVII, Propositions 2.3.2–2.3.3 and Proposition 3.5.4; Stacks Tag 00OK, algebra.tex, lemma-integral-sub-dim-equal

proof.text: For codimension zero the required equality is already equivariance of $B$ on geometric fibres. Indeed its three factors are morphisms on residue-field etale sites: the Gysin class of [lem-per-prime-power-regular-gysin], the natural tensor map of [lem-per-field-exceptional-tensor], and the canonical supported comparison of [lem-per-prime-power-supported-calculus]. A morphism on that site commutes with transport of its fibre: both orders send a section representing a germ to its image represented on the transported pointed neighbourhood. Their composite therefore commutes with the specified geometric transports. By [lem-per-higher-residue-transitivity] those transports are exactly the codimension-zero transitions. This also handles a nonidentity Galois automorphism; it is not asserted to act trivially.

source.place: XVII, Remark 1.4.2; Theorem 3.1.2 in codimension zero; Proposition 3.5.4

proof.text: The comparisons used here respect shifts and signed twists. For shifts, the three factors defining $B$ are maps of derived functors, so shifting the representing complex shifts each factor. For a twist $M(b)$ use the invertible rank-one Tate sheaf and the pullback, tensor and evaluation identifications of [lem-asd-etale-finite-twist-pullback]. Etale locally trivialize this line. The tensor map of [lem-per-field-exceptional-tensor] and the supported comparisons of [lem-per-prime-power-supported-calculus] then identify the formula for $B_{M(b)}$ with $B_M\otimes1$. Changing a trivialization multiplies both sides by the same unit, since the Gysin class and the other maps are $\Lambda$-linear. Hence this identification is canonical, including negative twists, whose identifications use evaluation. Immediate residues in [def-per-potential-dualizing-complex] use these same twist identifications and the termwise trait map. Thus their shifted and twisted squares are the squares for the shifted and twisted input. The higher squares below inherit these identifications by composition.

source.place: XVII, Sections 1.2.3 and 1.4; Definition 3.5.1; tensor and Gysin normalization in Proposition 2.4.3.1

proof.text:
Factor the specified arrow $\bar t'\rightsquigarrow\bar t$ into a finite chain $\bar t_0\rightsquigarrow\cdots\rightsquigarrow\bar t_r$, using [lem-per-higher-residue-transitivity]; retain its codimension-zero transports so that its composite is the actual specified geometric arrow. Set $\bar s_i=f\bar t_i$. Step 2 gives a projected factorization with the same successive codimensions $e_i\in\{0,1\}$. Put $d_i=\sum_{k<i}e_k$, $d_0=0$, and let $R_i^T,R_i^S$ be the transition composites up to index $i$, starting in degree $j$. For an immediate arrow, [lem-per-finite-residue-gysin-naturality], applied in degree $j+2d_i$ with input $M(d_i)$ and the identifications of Step 4, gives
$$r_i^T H^{j+2d_i}(B_{f,t_i,M}(d_i))=H^{j+2d_{i+1}}(B_{f,t_{i+1},M}(d_{i+1}))r_i^S.$$
For $e_i=0$ this is Step 3 with the same degree and twist. The hypotheses of the immediate lemma are satisfied on both schemes by Step 2; no potentiality or pointwise pinning is used.

source.place: XVII, Definition 3.5.1 and Proposition 3.5.4, first assertion, deduced from Proposition 3.3.1

proof.text:
Induct on $i$ to prove
$$R_i^T H^j(B_{f,t_0,M})=H^{j+2d_i}(B_{f,t_i,M}(d_i))R_i^S.$$
At $i=0$ both $R_0$ are identities. Given the equality at $i$, left-compose by $r_i^T$, substitute the edge equality of Step 5, and reassociate; this is exactly the equality at $i+1$. At $i=r$ one has $d_r=c$. By the composition and independence clauses of [lem-per-higher-residue-transitivity], $R_r^T$ and $R_r^S$ are the higher transitions for the original two geometric arrows. Substitution proves the displayed equation in the statement. For $c=0$ use Step 3 directly, or the same induction with only zero-codimension arrows. No cancellation of a residue map is made.

source.place: XVII, Proposition 3.5.4 and Theorem 3.1.2 (composition and independence of factorization)

proof.text: These comparisons are local for the restrictions asserted. For localization and strict localization, [lem-per-prime-power-supported-calculus] gives the exceptional restriction comparison, with its composition normalization; [lem-per-absolute-gysin-purity] gives the restriction of the Gysin class, and [lem-per-field-exceptional-tensor] fixes the tensor map and its composition law. Thus the three-factor definition of $B$ is unchanged under these identifications. For etale restriction the same assertion follows from exceptional transitivity: in a Cartesian etale restriction square with projections $u,v$ and finite map $f'$, identify $u^!f^!\cong f'^!v^!$ by the two expressions for the exceptional pullback of $fu=vf'$, then use the relative-dimension-zero comparisons $u^!=u^*$ and $v^!=v^*$ of [lem-per-noetherian-prime-power-smooth-duality]. This can be checked on separated affine etale neighbourhoods of the geometric points. Gysin etale compatibility and tensor composition identify the resulting costalk map with the same three-factor $B$, with no new scalar. The immediate transition is constructed on the strict local scheme in [def-per-potential-dualizing-complex]; an etale neighbourhood has the identical strict local scheme by [lem-trf-ind-etale-strict-local-invariance]. Hence its residue map is unchanged. Composing these immediate maps as in Steps 5–6 proves locality for higher transitions as well.

source.place: XVII, Proposition 2.2.1 and localization observation following it; Definitions 1.4.1 and 3.5.1; Proposition 3.5.4 and Lemma 3.5.5

proof.text: Finally suppose $f=i$ is a closed immersion. Its residue-field maps are identities, so their Gysin classes are identities by the identity compatibility in [lem-per-absolute-gysin-purity]. The tensor map for the identity is the identity, from its counit formula in [lem-per-field-exceptional-tensor]. The remaining factor of $B$ is therefore exactly the inverse supported-composition comparison $C_t(i^!M)\cong C_{i(t)}M$ of [lem-per-prime-power-supported-calculus]. Insert this description in Step 6. The resulting equality says precisely that supported composition identifies the two higher residue maps, including their twists and shifts; no regularity or purity assumption on the closed immersion is needed.

source.place: XVII, Proposition 3.5.4, closed-immersion case, and the reduction in Lemma 3.5.5

Purely inseparable: multiplication by [L:K], a unit, from the last clause of prime-power-regular-gysin. Its hypotheses are checked and injectivity is shown, not assumed. Step 3: c=0 transports commute with sheaf morphisms on kappa(t)_et; nontrivial Galois allowed. Step 4: shifts and signed twists via the asd twist identifications. Steps 5-6: the 3.3.1 square applied to M(d_i) in degree j+2d_i, then an induction with base case, successor step and composition/independence substitution; degrees and directions checked. Step 7: localization and strict localization via supported-calculus, Gysin and tensor restriction; etale restriction via transitivity and u^!=u^*; residue maps unchanged by ind-etale strict-local invariance. Step 8: closed immersion with Cl_id=1, T_id=1, leaving the supported comparison; no regularity used.
